Milestones in the history of chocolate.Olmecs use cacao: The Olmecs and later Maya and Aztecs prepared cacao as a bitter, frothy drink, and the Aztecs even used the beans as currency.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Van Houten's cocoa press: Coenraad van Houten's press separated cocoa butter from the powder, making cocoa cheaper and creating the base for modern chocolate.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Fry's first chocolate bar: The British firm Fry's made the first mass-produced edible bar by mixing cocoa powder, sugar and cocoa butter.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Milk chocolate: Daniel Peter of Switzerland invented milk chocolate with help from Henri Nestlé, who had developed condensed milk.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Lindt invents conching: Rodolphe Lindt's technique of stirring the chocolate for hours creates its silky texture, and it still defines premium chocolate.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Hershey's Kisses: Milton Hershey's bite-sized foil-wrapped chocolates got their name, supposedly from the sound they made as they dropped from the machine.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Mars bar: This bar of nougat and caramel covered in chocolate was created by Forrest Mars, and the brand became one of the best known.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.White chocolate bar: Nestlé introduced the first white chocolate, made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk, but no cocoa solids.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Chocolate fondue: The Swiss chef Konrad Egli invented this dessert at his New York restaurant, Chalet Suisse.
Milestones in the history of chocolate.Ruby chocolate: Barry Callebaut introduced the pink chocolate, said to be the first new variety of chocolate in about 80 years.

Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Richard III: Opens with 'Now is the winter of our discontent', and the play helped shape his villainous reputation.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Romeo and Juliet: Based on a poem by Arthur Brooke, set in Verona, with feuding families whose children fall in love.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.The Merchant of Venice: Features Shylock and gave English the idiom 'a pound of flesh'.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Julius Caesar: Likely among the first plays at the Globe Theatre, which opened in 1599, per a visitor's account.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Hamlet: Shakespeare's longest play, at about 4,000 lines, with the famous 'To be or not to be' soliloquy.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Othello: Based on an Italian tale by Cinthio, and Iago actually has more lines than Othello himself.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.King Lear: In 1681 Nahum Tate gave it a happy ending, and that version replaced the original on stage for about 150 years.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Coriolanus: The late tragedy of a Roman general who turns on Rome, echoing grain riots in England in 1607.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.The Tempest: Often thought the last play he wrote alone, and Prospero's farewell to magic is sometimes read as Shakespeare's own.
Shakespeare plays, by when he wrote them.Henry VIII: During a 1613 performance, a cannon shot set the Globe's thatched roof on fire and burned the theatre down.

Famous observatories from north to south.Jodrell Bank (UK): This giant radio telescope near Manchester tracked Sputnik's rocket in 1957 and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Famous observatories from north to south.Royal Observatory Greenwich: The prime meridian, zero longitude, passes through here; it was founded in 1675 to help sailors find longitude.
Famous observatories from north to south.Yerkes Observatory: Home to the world's largest refracting telescope, with a 40-inch lens, since 1897.
Famous observatories from north to south.Palomar Observatory: Its 200-inch Hale telescope was the largest in the world from 1948 to 1975.
Famous observatories from north to south.Mauna Kea Observatories: Its summit stands at over 4,000 meters, above much of the atmosphere's water vapor, and houses the twin Keck telescopes.
Famous observatories from north to south.Arecibo Observatory: The 305-meter dish in Puerto Rico beamed the 1974 message toward the stars before it collapsed in December 2020.
Famous observatories from north to south.ALMA (Chile): This array of 66 antennas sits at about 5,000 meters in the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth.
Famous observatories from north to south.Paranal Observatory: Home to the Very Large Telescope, this site in Chile also doubled as a villain's hideout in the James Bond film Quantum of Solace.
Famous observatories from north to south.SALT (South Africa): The largest single optical telescope in the southern hemisphere, its mirror is about 11 meters wide, and it sits in the Karoo.
Famous observatories from north to south.South Pole Telescope: The 10-meter dish at the Amundsen-Scott station studies the cosmic microwave background through months of polar night.

NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Alfa: It is spelled without ph so that speakers of any language will pronounce it correctly, as the whole code is designed for clarity over bad radio lines.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Echo: The alphabet was tested on speakers of many languages in the 1950s, and words like Echo were chosen for being easy to hear and say worldwide.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Hotel: Radio operators and pilots use it to separate H from similar-sounding letters over crackly lines.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Kilo: Kilo comes from the Greek for thousand, as in kilogram, and the NATO alphabet's official pronunciation stresses the first syllable: KEY-loh.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Lima: It is named for the capital of Peru, one of only two place names in the alphabet along with Quebec.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Oscar: Oscar is one of several personal names in the code, along with Romeo, Victor and Juliett.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Quebec: Pronounced keh-BECK, as in the Canadian province, it is the second place name in the alphabet, with Lima.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Tango: The dance began in Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the 19th century, and UNESCO listed tango as cultural heritage in 2009.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Whiskey: The alphabet spells it with an e, though Scotland and Canada spell the drink as whisky.
NATO phonetic alphabet, in order.Zulu: Zulu also means Greenwich time in the military and aviation, so 1400Z is 2 pm in Greenwich.

Birth flowers through the year.Carnation: Its botanical name Dianthus means divine flower, and in the US it is tied to Mother's Day.
Birth flowers through the year.Violet: Victorian sweethearts exchanged violets as a sign of faithfulness, and their scent briefly vanishes because ionone numbs the nose.
Birth flowers through the year.Daffodil: Wordsworth's I wandered lonely as a cloud made it famous, though every part of the plant is poisonous to eat.
Birth flowers through the year.Lily of the valley: Tiny, fragrant and highly poisonous, it is given in France on 1 May as a lucky charm.
Birth flowers through the year.Rose: Fossils show roses grew about 35 million years ago, long before humans appeared.
Birth flowers through the year.Larkspur: Its tall spikes are toxic to cattle, and it is named for the spur resembling a lark's claw.
Birth flowers through the year.Gladiolus: Its name comes from the Latin gladius, a sword, for its blade-shaped leaves.
Birth flowers through the year.Aster: Its name is Greek for star, which is the shape of its flower.
Birth flowers through the year.Marigold: In Mexico's Day of the Dead, cempasuchil marigolds guide spirits home with colour and scent.
Birth flowers through the year.Chrysanthemum: In Japan it is the imperial emblem, and the Chrysanthemum Throne is a name for the monarchy itself.

Mammal numbers trivia.Pouches on a kangaroo: Kangaroos have one pouch, and the baby, called a joey, is born about the size of a jellybean and crawls into it unaided.
Mammal numbers trivia.Horns on a black rhino: Black rhinos have two horns, and the front one is longer; both are made of keratin, the same protein as our hair and nails.
Mammal numbers trivia.Stomach chambers in a camel: Camels have three stomach compartments, and contrary to myth their humps store fat, not water.
Mammal numbers trivia.Chambers in a mammal's heart: Mammals' hearts have four chambers, and that separation of oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood helps them stay warm-blooded.
Mammal numbers trivia.Molar sets an elephant gets: An elephant grows six sets of molars across its life, and when the last set wears out, it can starve.
Mammal numbers trivia.Teats on a Virginia opossum: Virginia opossums have 13 teats arranged in a ring of 12 with one in the middle, and litters can be bigger than that number.
Mammal numbers trivia.Whiskers on a cat: A cat's whiskers act like sensors that help it judge gaps, and they are about as wide as the cat's body.
Mammal numbers trivia.Muscles in a cat's ear: Cats can rotate their ears independently, thanks to many muscles, which helps them pinpoint the faintest rustle.
Mammal numbers trivia.Muscles in a human body: Muscles make up about 40 percent of body weight, and the largest is the gluteus maximus in the buttocks.
Mammal numbers trivia.Quills on a porcupine: Porcupine quills are modified hairs, and contrary to myth they can't be shot, but they detach easily when touched.

Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Aeschylus: Aeschylus is called the father of Greek tragedy, and he fought at Marathon, and he reportedly died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his head.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Sophocles: Sophocles wrote Oedipus Rex, and he won the festival of Dionysus in Athens roughly 20 times.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Euripides: Euripides gave his characters realistic psychology, and he wrote Medea, which shocked audiences.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Aristophanes: Aristophanes was the leading master of Greek comedy, and his play Lysistrata imagines women going on a sex strike to end a war.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Menander: Menander wrote New Comedy, and its stock characters and plots fed straight into the sitcoms we watch.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Plautus: Plautus was a Roman comic playwright whose stories were adapted into the musical A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Terence: Terence was brought to Rome as an enslaved person, and he was freed to write comedies praised for their polished Latin.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Seneca: Seneca was Nero's tutor, and his bloody tragedies influenced Elizabethan dramatists such as Shakespeare.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Kalidasa: Kalidasa is called India's Shakespeare, and his play Shakuntala so impressed Goethe that he wrote a poem about it.
Dramatists of the ancient and old world,.Zeami (Noh master): Zeami wrote and perfected the Noh theatre, and his treatises on acting are still studied in Japan.

US cities from north to south.Anchorage: Alaska's biggest city is far enough north to see midnight twilight in summer and just about five and a half hours of daylight in December.
US cities from north to south.Fargo: Fargo, North Dakota was a Northern Pacific Railway stop, and its name was borrowed by the Coen brothers' dark-comedy film, though most of that movie takes place in Minnesota.
US cities from north to south.Minneapolis: Minneapolis is a city of lakes, and it is among the most northerly of the major US cities; its river-mills made it the 'Flour Milling Capital' once.
US cities from north to south.Boston: Boston's latitude is about the same as that of Rome, Italy, and the two cities also share a similar climate sometimes in summer.
US cities from north to south.Denver: Denver is called the Mile High City because its official elevation is 5,280 feet, and a marked step in the Capitol shows the exact mile.
US cities from north to south.San Francisco: San Francisco's fog, called Karl, rolls in from the Pacific, and the Golden Gate Bridge's color is officially 'International Orange'.
US cities from north to south.Los Angeles: Los Angeles gets only about 36 cm of rain a year, close to desert levels, so it relies on water piped in from distant mountains and rivers.
US cities from north to south.Dallas: Dallas grew as a cotton and railroad hub, and with neighboring Fort Worth it forms one of the largest metro areas in the country.
US cities from north to south.Miami: Miami's highest natural ground is only a few meters above sea level, so rising seas and floods are an unusually big concern here.
US cities from north to south.Honolulu: Honolulu is the southernmost state capital in the United States, and it lies in the tropics, at about 21 degrees north.

When these cities opened their first met.London: London opened the world's first underground passenger railway, steam-powered, between Paddington and Farringdon, and carried tens of thousands on day one.
When these cities opened their first met.Budapest: The Budapest line was the first electric underground in continental Europe, built to celebrate the Hungarian Millennium.
When these cities opened their first met.Paris: Paris's first line opened just in time for the 1900 World's Fair, and its curving art-nouveau entrances were designed by Hector Guimard.
When these cities opened their first met.Berlin: The Berlin U-Bahn began with an elevated stretch before diving underground, and parts of the system were divided by the Wall during the Cold War.
When these cities opened their first met.New York: The New York subway's first line ran from City Hall to Harlem, and its tiled stations were designed to feel grand rather than purely practical.
When these cities opened their first met.Buenos Aires: Buenos Aires built the first subway in Latin America and the Southern Hemisphere, and its oldest cars stayed in service for about a century.
When these cities opened their first met.Tokyo: Tokyo's Ginza Line was the first subway in Asia, funded by a businessman who famously counted pedestrians to gauge demand.
When these cities opened their first met.Moscow: The Moscow Metro was built as a showpiece of Soviet ambition, with chandeliers, mosaics and marble in stations nicknamed 'people's palaces'.
When these cities opened their first met.Mexico City: Mexico City's metro uses pictograms for every station so that people who could not read could still find their way, such as a grasshopper for Chapultepec.
The Washington Metro opened in time for the nation's bicentennial and is known for its dramatic coffered concrete vaults.

Count these classic game components.Dice in Yahtzee: Yahtzee uses five dice, and the name was a registered trademark; the game was originally called 'The Yacht Game'.
Count these classic game components.Continents in Risk: Risk has six continents, and Australia is easiest to defend because it has only one entry point.
Count these classic game components.Rooms in Clue: Clue has nine rooms, and the murder mystery was invented in Britain during the Second World War as 'Cluedo'.
Count these classic game components.Hotels in Monopoly: Monopoly has 12 hotels per set, but the supply is limited, and that limit is important to strategy.
Count these classic game components.Boxes on a Yahtzee scorecard: A Yahtzee scorecard has 13 boxes, which means a game ends after exactly 13 turns.
Count these classic game components.Terrain hexes in Catan: Catan's board has 19 terrain hexes, and was invented in Germany by a dental technician, Klaus Teuber.
Count these classic game components.Properties in Monopoly: Monopoly has 28 properties, including 22 streets, four railroads and two utilities.
Count these classic game components.Houses in Monopoly: Monopoly has 32 houses, and in 1973 the housing shortage was a real feature in the game, because players could run out of them.
Count these classic game components.Territories in Risk: Risk has 42 territories, each with a card, and the game was created by a French film director, Albert Lamorisse.
Count these classic game components.Numbers in US bingo: US bingo uses numbers from 1 to 75, split into five columns labelled B-I-N-G-O, and the game started with a Georgia toy salesman.

British money slang, by value.A bob: Pre-decimal money had the shilling; though its source is unknown, you still hear a few bob in British talk.
British money slang, by value.A Lady Godiva: It rhymes with fiver and refers to the Coventry noblewoman who legendarily rode naked through town in protest at taxes.
British money slang, by value.An Ayrton Senna: It rhymes with tenner and honors the Brazilian Formula One champion.
British money slang, by value.A score: Score for twenty comes from old counting by notches, as in Lincoln's four score and seven years.
British money slang, by value.A pony: Its origin is uncertain, but pony and monkey are both bookmakers' and gamblers' slang from the 19th century.
British money slang, by value.A bullseye: The slang comes from the 50 points awarded for hitting the bullseye on a dartboard.
British money slang, by value.A ton: The word ton also means 100 in doing a ton, riding a motorbike at 100 mph.
British money slang, by value.A monkey: Its origin is debated; theories range from Indian rupees to old gambling slang, but nobody knows for sure.
British money slang, by value.A grand: Grand became slang for a thousand in the US around the 1920s before crossing the Atlantic.
British money slang, by value.An Archer: It refers to novelist and politician Jeffrey Archer, who was jailed for perjury after a case involving a £2,000 payment.

When these rhythm games came out.PaRappa the Rapper: Masaya Matsuura created this rapping-dog game, often credited as the first big rhythm game for PlayStation.
When these rhythm games came out.Beatmania: Konami's arcade game used a turntable controller, and it launched the whole Bemani line of music games.
When these rhythm games came out.Dance Dance Revolution: Players hit arrows with their feet on a dance pad; it turned arcades into dance floors.
When these rhythm games came out.Taiko no Tatsujin: Namco's drum game has players hit the drum for 'don' and the rim for 'katsu', with real drum controllers.
When these rhythm games came out.SingStar: This karaoke game for PlayStation 2 scored singers on pitch, and was developed by Sony in London.
When these rhythm games came out.Guitar Hero: Harmonix's guitar-controller game had RedOctane publishing it, and Harmonix later made Rock Band.
When these rhythm games came out.Rock Band: It added drums, vocals and bass so that a whole band could play together, and it later had a Beatles edition.
When these rhythm games came out.Just Dance: Ubisoft's dance game tracked the Wii remote in your hand, so you didn't need a dance mat.
When these rhythm games came out.Rocksmith: You plug in a real electric guitar with a cable, learning actual chords instead of pressing coloured buttons.
When these rhythm games came out.Beat Saber: In this VR game you slice cubes with lightsabers in time to the music, and Meta bought its Czech maker in 2019.

Big ideas about the cosmos.Aristarchus: Sun at center: The Greek astronomer proposed a Sun-centered system about 1,800 years before Copernicus, but few accepted it.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Ptolemy's Almagest: The name is Arabic for "the greatest". Ptolemy's Earth-centered model ruled astronomy for more than 1,400 years.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Copernicus's model: His book appeared in the year he died. Legend says he was handed a printed copy on his deathbed.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Halley predicts his comet: He saw that comets in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object and predicted its return in 1758, but he did not live to see it.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Herschel finds infrared: William Herschel found it by measuring heat beyond the red end of a prism's spectrum. He also discovered Uranus in 1781.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Universe is expanding: Edwin Hubble showed galaxies recede, the more distant ones faster, building on earlier work by Georges Lemaitre.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Big Bang afterglow found: Penzias and Wilson first heard it as a persistent hiss in a horn antenna, and even blamed pigeon droppings. It won them a Nobel.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Planet around a Sun-like star: The planet 51 Pegasi b was a hot Jupiter circling its star in about four days. Its discoverers won the 2019 Nobel Prize.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Pluto reclassified: An International Astronomical Union vote created the class of dwarf planets, and Clyde Tombaugh's 1930 discovery lost its planet status.
Big ideas about the cosmos.Gravitational waves detected: LIGO caught two black holes merging over a billion years ago, a century after Einstein predicted gravitational waves.

Famous paintings, by canvas size.The Persistence of Memory: Salvador Dalí painted it in 1931, and he said the melting clocks were inspired by Camembert cheese running in the sun.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.Girl with a Pearl Earring: A 'tronie' by Vermeer, meaning a character study rather than a portrait, with a turban painted in precious ultramarine.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.Mona Lisa: It was painted on a poplar wood panel rather than canvas, and is far smaller than most visitors expect.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.The Starry Night: Van Gogh painted it in 1889 from memory during his stay at the asylum at Saint-Rémy, inspired by the view from his window.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.The Birth of Venus: Botticelli painted it on canvas, then unusual in Florence, instead of the wood panels used for most pictures.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.Las Meninas: Velázquez put himself in the picture at his easel, and Picasso later painted 58 variations of it.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.The Night Watch: Trimmed on all sides in 1715 to fit a wall, and its title came from darkened varnish that made the daylight scene look like night.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.Guernica: Picasso painted it after the 1937 bombing of the Basque town; it stayed abroad until Spain returned to democracy.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.The Last Supper: Leonardo painted it as a mural on dry plaster, an experimental technique, which began to flake within years.
Famous paintings, by canvas size.The Wedding at Cana: Veronese's vast painting hangs in the Louvre directly opposite the Mona Lisa, and was taken from Venice by Napoleon's army.

Pixar's first ten films, by release.Toy Story: It was the first feature film made entirely with computer animation, and Disney distributed it.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.A Bug's Life: Its end-credit bloopers were a first for animated films, and it came out the same year as DreamWorks' rival ant film, Antz.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.Toy Story 2: Nearly erased by an accidental command, it was rescued by a backup an employee kept at home, then rewritten in months.
Sulley had about 2.3 million individual hairs, a record at the time for computer-animated fur.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.Finding Nemo: It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and the clownfish-anemone partnership shown in it is real.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.The Incredibles: Brad Bird's superhero family film won two Oscars, and Edna Mode's rule, no capes, became a fan favorite.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.Cars: It was inspired by Route 66, and Radiator Springs borrows from real towns like Peach Springs, Arizona, and Galena, Kansas.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.Ratatouille: Chef Thomas Keller designed the confit byaldi dish shown in the film, a fancier take on the vegetable stew.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.WALL-E: The first forty minutes have almost no dialogue, and sound designer Ben Burtt, who made R2-D2's beeps, created WALL-E's voice.
Pixar's first ten films, by release.Up: It was Pixar's first film in 3D and the first animated film to open the Cannes Film Festival.

When these ancient battles were fought.Megiddo: Thutmose III's victory over a Canaanite coalition was the first battle recorded in detail, and its site's name gave us Armageddon.
When these ancient battles were fought.Qarqar: Assyria's Shalmaneser III faced a coalition including Ahab of Israel, and the record contains the first mention of Arabs in history.
When these ancient battles were fought.Thermopylae: Leonidas and a small Greek force, including 300 Spartans, held the pass against Xerxes for days until a local showed the Persians a hidden path.
When these ancient battles were fought.Leuctra: Thebes, under Epaminondas, broke Sparta's aura of invincibility using an extra-deep left flank.
When these ancient battles were fought.Issus: Alexander routed Darius III, who fled, leaving his family behind to be captured.
When these ancient battles were fought.Ipsus: Alexander's successors fought it out; Antigonus died, and it ended hopes of reuniting the empire, with war elephants helping Seleucus.
When these ancient battles were fought.Zama: Scipio Africanus beat Hannibal in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War.
When these ancient battles were fought.Pydna: The Roman legion beat the Macedonian phalanx, ending the kingdom of Macedon.
When these ancient battles were fought.Carrhae: Crassus's legions fell to Parthian horse archers, and legend says the Parthians poured molten gold down his throat.
When these ancient battles were fought.Philippi: Antony and Octavian beat Brutus and Cassius, Caesar's assassins, who both took their own lives.

Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.yocto-: The smallest SI prefix, added in 1991, comes from the Latin "octo", eight, as it is the eighth power of a thousand. A proton weighs about 1.7 yoctograms.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.zepto-: Added in 1991 along with yocto, and built from the Latin "septem", seven. In 2020 physicists timed light crossing a molecule in about 247 zeptoseconds.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.atto-: From the Danish word for "eighteen". Attosecond laser pulses can freeze the motion of electrons, and won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.femto-: From the Danish for "fifteen". A femtometer is about the size of a proton, and ultrafast chemistry is studied with femtosecond laser flashes.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.pico-: This prefix means a trillionth. In one picosecond, light travels only about 0.3 millimeters, less than the thickness of a credit card.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.nano-: From the Greek for "dwarf". A human hair is roughly 80,000 nanometers wide, and modern computer chips have features measured in nanometers.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.micro-: From the Greek for "small". A micrometer is about the size of a typical bacterium, and about one-fiftieth of a hair's width.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.milli-: From the Latin for "thousand", as in millimeter, which is about the thickness of a coin, and milliliter, of which a liter holds 1,000.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.centi-: From the Latin for "hundred". A centimeter is about the width of a fingernail, and it is a rare prefix that is not a power of 1,000.
Tiny SI prefixes, by the size they mean.deci-: From the Latin for "ten". It's best known in decibel, a tenth of a bel, a unit named for Alexander Graham Bell.

Roald Dahl books, by publication.James and the Giant Peach: It was published in the US in 1961, six years before it appeared in Britain.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.Charlie (Chocolate Factory): Dahl drew on 1920s chocolate firms, such as Cadbury and Rowntree, who spied on each other's recipes.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.Fantastic Mr Fox: Wes Anderson turned it into a stop-motion film in 2009.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.Danny the Champion: A boy and his father poach pheasants in an English countryside much like Dahl's own home near Great Missenden.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.The Twits: Quentin Blake's scribbly illustrations helped define the look of Dahl's books.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.George's Marvellous Medicine: The brew in which a boy mixes shampoo, paint and animal pills for his grumpy grandmother shows Dahl's glee at defying nagging adults.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.The BFG: Dahl invented dozens of words for it, such as 'snozzcumber' and 'whizzpopping', and dedicated the book to his late daughter Olivia.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.The Witches: Anjelica Huston played the Grand High Witch in the 1990 film, whose ending differed from the book's.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.Matilda: Tim Minchin wrote the songs for the hit stage musical that premiered with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 2010.
Roald Dahl books, by publication.Esio Trot: The title is 'tortoise' spelled backwards, and it was among the last books published before Dahl died in 1990.

Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Fridge: A fridge is held just above freezing, around 37 degrees F, since cold slows bacteria's growth, although it does not stop it altogether.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Proofing dough: Dough rises fastest in a warm, slightly humid spot, as yeast gets active at around 85, and above 140 degrees it dies.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Dehydrating fruit: Fruit dehydrators run at this low heat for hours, drying fruit without cooking it, so the sugars concentrate and the pieces turn chewy.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Keeping plates warm: Restaurants keep plates in a low oven at this heat, and this temperature is also hot enough to keep food out of the danger zone.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Smoking brisket: Low and slow cooking melts the tough collagen in brisket into gelatin, which takes many hours and produces the famous tender texture.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Baking cookies: Cookies bake at this common temperature as the heat sets the edges before the middle dries out, and sugar caramelises into golden colour.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Roasting vegetables: High heat browns vegetables through caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, which brings out sweetness that steaming never reaches.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Home-oven pizza: Home ovens struggle to match pizzerias, and many people put a heated stone or steel in to get closer to the crisp crust.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Broiler: The broiler's heat comes from above, much like a grill turned upside down, and it browns tops of dishes in minutes.
Fahrenheit settings: from fridge to wood.Wood-fired pizza oven: Neapolitan pizzas cook in about 60 to 90 seconds at this temperature, giving blistered, charred crust and a soft, chewy centre.

Birds on the scale.Bee hummingbird: This Cuban native is the smallest bird, with a heart that beats over 1,000 times a minute and a nest the size of a thimble.
Birds on the scale.House sparrow: It followed humans around the world, but has been declining in parts of Europe for decades.
Birds on the scale.American robin: Not related to the European robin, it is actually a thrush, named by homesick colonists for the bird back home.
Birds on the scale.Rock pigeon: The ancestor of city pigeons, it has a strong homing instinct that made homing pigeons wartime messengers.
Birds on the scale.Mallard: The ancestor of most domestic ducks, the male has the famous glossy green head.
Birds on the scale.Chicken (hen): The domestic chicken descends from red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, and there are over 20 billion of them, more than any other bird.
Birds on the scale.Bald eagle: It isn't bald; the name comes from an old sense of 'white', and it builds the biggest nests of any North American bird.
Birds on the scale.Mute swan: Despite the name it hisses and snorts, and in England the Crown claims ownership of unmarked ones.
Birds on the scale.Emu: Males of this flightless Australian bird sit on the eggs for about eight weeks, barely eating.
Birds on the scale.Ostrich: The biggest living bird has the largest eyes of any land animal, and it does not really bury its head in sand.

Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Newcomen steam engine: It pumped water out of coal mines and burned so much coal itself that it was used mostly at the mines.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Flying shuttle: John Kay's invention made weaving so fast that spinners couldn't keep up with the yarn supply.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Spinning jenny: Credited to James Hargreaves, it spun several threads at once, and weavers feared for their jobs.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Watt's separate condenser: The separate condenser made engines far more efficient, and the unit of power is named for him.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Spinning mule: Samuel Crompton's machine was a hybrid of two earlier ones, hence the name mule.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Power loom: Edmund Cartwright, a clergyman with no weaving experience, invented it.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Cotton gin: Eli Whitney's machine made cotton so profitable that it entrenched slavery in the American South.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Fulton's Clermont steamboat: Robert Fulton's boat was the first commercially successful steamboat, going from New York to Albany in about 32 hours.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Stephenson's Rocket: It won the 1829 Rainhill trials, reaching about 48 km/h.
Machines of the Industrial Revolution.Bessemer steel process: Blowing air through molten iron made steel cheap, and it became the metal of rails and skyscrapers.

3D shapes by number of faces.Tetrahedron: The simplest Platonic solid is made of four triangles, and it is the only one that has no parallel faces.
3D shapes by number of faces.Square pyramid: The Egyptian pyramids are this shape, one square base and four triangular sides.
3D shapes by number of faces.Cube: On a standard die, opposite faces always add up to seven.
3D shapes by number of faces.Pentagonal prism: Two pentagons are joined by five rectangles, and a prism is any solid with two matching ends and flat sides.
3D shapes by number of faces.Octahedron: Diamonds often grow as octahedral crystals, and the shape is made of eight triangles.
3D shapes by number of faces.Heptagonal prism: A heptagon has seven sides, and the UK's 50p coin has a seven-sided curved outline.
3D shapes by number of faces.Dodecahedron: Plato linked the dodecahedron's twelve pentagons to the cosmos, since it was the only solid left over after he assigned the others to elements.
3D shapes by number of faces.Icosahedron: Many viruses, including adenovirus, form this twenty-triangle shape, and it is also the die used in role-playing games.
3D shapes by number of faces.Classic soccer ball shape: Technically a truncated icosahedron made of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons; the same shape as the carbon molecule buckyball.
3D shapes by number of faces.Rhombicosidodecahedron: This Archimedean solid combines 20 triangles, 30 squares and 12 pentagons, in a shape that has been known since Kepler's time.

From pocket-size to towering.Oscar statuette: The Oscar, 34 cm tall and about 3.9 kg, is gold-plated bronze, and its official name is the Academy Award of Merit.
From pocket-size to towering.Manneken Pis: This little Brussels fountain statue of a boy is often dressed in costumes, and has a wardrobe of over a thousand outfits.
From pocket-size to towering.Stanley Cup: Named for Lord Stanley, Canada's Governor General, who donated it in 1892; winners' names are engraved on it and each player gets a day with it.
From pocket-size to towering.One Hollywood sign letter: It first read Hollywoodland in 1923, as a real-estate advertisement; the land was dropped in 1949.
From pocket-size to towering.A Mount Rushmore face: Sculptor Gutzon Borglum led about 400 workers who blasted away roughly 450,000 tons of rock to carve the four presidents.
From pocket-size to towering.Christ the Redeemer (statue): This 30 m statue stands on Corcovado mountain above Rio, is made of reinforced concrete covered in soapstone tiles, and was finished in 1931.
From pocket-size to towering.Statue of Liberty (no base): Its copper skin is only about 2.4 mm thick and turned green by oxidation; Gustave Eiffel designed the iron skeleton inside.
From pocket-size to towering.Leaning Tower of Pisa: It began tilting during construction because of soft ground; engineers straightened it by about 40 cm by 2001.
From pocket-size to towering.Big Ben's tower: Big Ben is the name of the bell, not the tower, which is called the Elizabeth Tower, renamed in 2012 for the Queen's Diamond Jubilee.
From pocket-size to towering.Eiffel Tower: Built for the 1889 World's Fair and meant to stand 20 years, it was saved by its use as a radio antenna; it grows a few centimeters in summer heat.

How tall are these statues?.The Little Mermaid: Copenhagen's bronze statue of Andersen's heroine was commissioned by brewer Carl Jacobsen, and has been beheaded and vandalized more than once.
How tall are these statues?.Michelangelo's David: Michelangelo carved it from a flawed block of marble other sculptors had abandoned, finishing in his late twenties.
How tall are these statues?.Tallest moai (Paro): Paro weighs about 82 tonnes and is the tallest moai known to have been erected on Easter Island.
How tall are these statues?.Great Sphinx of Giza: Carved from a limestone outcrop, the lion-bodied figure is about 73 m long, and ancient sand often buried it.
How tall are these statues?.The Kelpies: These giant steel horse heads near Falkirk, Scotland, honour the working horses of the country's industrial past.
How tall are these statues?.Leshan Giant Buddha: Carved into a Sichuan cliff over about 90 years from AD 713, it was meant to calm dangerous river waters.
How tall are these statues?.The Motherland Calls: Overlooking Volgograd, formerly Stalingrad, it commemorates the Battle of Stalingrad, and its raised sword is over 30 m long.
How tall are these statues?.Peter the Great (Moscow): Zurab Tsereteli's 1997 monument is polarizing, and Muscovites have often petitioned for its removal.
How tall are these statues?.Spring Temple Buddha: This Henan statue was the world's tallest until 2018, when the Statue of Unity surpassed it.
How tall are these statues?.Statue of Unity: In Gujarat, it honours Sardar Patel, who united India's princely states, and stands roughly twice as tall as the Statue of Liberty.

Music, by how long it takes to play.Flight of the Bumblebee: It comes from Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan, where a prince magically turns into a bee to fly to his father.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Cage's 4′33″: No notes are played at all. The 'music' is the ambient noise of the hall. David Tudor premiered it in 1952.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Ravel's Boléro: Ravel's ballet piece repeats one theme and rhythm while gradually adding instruments and volume. He called it an experiment in orchestration.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Vivaldi's Four Seasons: A set of four violin concertos, each paired with a sonnet describing the season, such as storms, hunting and frozen winter.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Beethoven's Ninth Symphony: The first major symphony to include voices. Its 'Ode to Joy' became the anthem of the European Union.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Mahler's Third Symphony: Often called the longest symphony in the standard repertoire, its first movement alone can last about half an hour.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Handel's Messiah: Handel's oratorio premiered in Dublin in 1742. Audiences traditionally stand for the 'Hallelujah' chorus.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Götterdämmerung: The last opera of Wagner's Ring cycle, its title means 'Twilight of the Gods', and it ends with the destruction of Valhalla.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Wagner's full Ring cycle: Four operas written over about 26 years, performed in a theatre Wagner designed himself at Bayreuth.
Music, by how long it takes to play.Cage's ASLSP (Halberstadt): The title stands for 'As Slow As Possible'. A church performance in Halberstadt began in 2001 and is due to end in 2640.

The 1960s, one event per year.JFK elected: At 43 he became the youngest person ever elected president and the first Catholic, narrowly beating Nixon after televised debates.
The 1960s, one event per year.Berlin Wall built: East Germany raised it overnight to stop people fleeing west; it ringed West Berlin for about 155 km and stood until 1989.
The 1960s, one event per year.Cuban Missile Crisis: A tense 13-day standoff over Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers closest to nuclear war, ending when the missiles were withdrawn.
The 1960s, one event per year.March on Washington: About 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech.
The 1960s, one event per year.Gulf of Tonkin incident: Reported attacks on US destroyers off Vietnam led Congress to authorize escalating the war; one of the reported attacks probably never happened.
The 1960s, one event per year.Voting Rights Act: It outlawed literacy tests and other tricks used to keep Black Americans from voting, after the Selma marches pushed Congress to act.
The 1960s, one event per year.Cultural Revolution begins: Mao launched it to purge rivals and 'bourgeois' ideas; Red Guards attacked teachers and officials, and schools closed for years.
The 1960s, one event per year.Six-Day War: Israel's lightning strike against Egypt, Jordan and Syria seized Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank and the Golan Heights, reshaping the region.
The 1960s, one event per year.MLK assassinated: He was shot in Memphis while supporting striking sanitation workers, and riots erupted in many US cities afterward.
The 1960s, one event per year.Moon landing: Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above; hundreds of millions watched on television.

Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Iodine: The thyroid needs it to make hormones, which is why iodine is added to table salt in many countries.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Iron: Most of the metal sits in haemoglobin, about the weight of a small nail in total, and it carries oxygen.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Sodium: It helps nerves fire and fluids balance, and it comes mainly from salt.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Potassium: Our potassium includes a tiny radioactive fraction, so every person is slightly radioactive.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Phosphorus: Most of it forms the mineral in bones and teeth, but it also sits in DNA and the cell's energy molecule ATP.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Calcium: About 99 percent of it is in bones and teeth, with the rest used in muscles and nerves.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Nitrogen: It is in every protein and in DNA, yet we can't use the air's nitrogen and must get it from food.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Hydrogen: Only about seven kilograms by mass, but hydrogen makes up around 60 percent of all atoms in your body.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Carbon: This is the backbone of every organic molecule, making up almost a fifth of your body weight.
Elements in a 70 kg human body, by mass.Oxygen: Most of it is locked up in water, which makes up around 60 percent of an adult's body.

Great earthquakes through history.Lisbon: It struck on All Saints' Day, followed by a tsunami and fires, and it shook European faith and fed Voltaire's Candide.
Great earthquakes through history.San Francisco: Fires that followed did much of the damage, and about 3,000 people died.
Great earthquakes through history.Great Kantō (Tokyo): Tokyo and Yokohama were struck at lunchtime, and over 100,000 died, mainly in firestorms.
Great earthquakes through history.Valdivia, Chile: It was a magnitude 9.5, the strongest ever recorded, and the tsunami crossed the entire Pacific.
Great earthquakes through history.Tangshan, China: It struck at night and the official toll was about 240,000, one of the deadliest earthquakes in modern times.
Great earthquakes through history.Kobe, Japan: Known in Japan as the Great Hanshin earthquake, it killed more than 6,000 people and spurred stricter building codes.
Great earthquakes through history.Indian Ocean tsunami quake: A magnitude 9.1 quake sent waves that killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries.
Great earthquakes through history.Haiti: A shallow magnitude 7.0 quake hit near Port-au-Prince and killed well over 100,000.
Great earthquakes through history.Tōhoku, Japan: The magnitude 9.0 quake and tsunami also triggered the nuclear accident at Fukushima Daiichi.
Great earthquakes through history.Turkey–Syria: Two huge quakes, about nine hours apart, struck southern Turkey and northern Syria and killed more than 50,000 people.

How many teeth does an adult have?.Giant anteater: Its tongue can reach about 60 cm and flicks in and out around 150 times a minute to catch ants and termites.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Narwhal: The tusk is actually an overgrown left canine that spirals through the lip and is packed with nerve endings.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Rabbit: A second tiny pair of 'peg teeth' sits behind its front incisors, one thing that sets rabbits apart from rodents.
How many teeth does an adult have?.House cat: Kittens have only 26 baby teeth, which fall out around six months to make way for the adult set.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Human: Many adults have fewer than the full set because some never develop their wisdom teeth.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Dog: Puppies are born toothless and get 28 baby teeth, which are replaced by this larger adult set.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Virginia opossum: With 50, it has more teeth than any other North American land mammal, a legacy of ancient marsupial ancestors.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Bottlenose dolphin: Its cone-shaped teeth only grab fish, which it swallows whole, and it can use them without chewing.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Great white shark: Rows of spare teeth rotate forward like a conveyor belt, and one shark may use thousands in a lifetime.
How many teeth does an adult have?.Garden snail: A snail's tongue-like radula is a ribbon covered in rows of tiny teeth, which rasp food into bits.

When these ancient scientists were born.Pythagoras: The Greek thinker of Samos founded a secretive school in Croton, and is credited with a theorem Babylonians had already used.
When these ancient scientists were born.Hippocrates: Called the Father of Medicine, he taught on Kos, and doctors still take an oath that bears his name.
When these ancient scientists were born.Archimedes: Legend says he shouted 'Eureka!' after noticing his bath overflow, when he grasped how to measure the volume of an irregular object.
When these ancient scientists were born.Hipparchus: He compiled one of the first star catalogues and discovered the precession of the equinoxes, the slow wobble of Earth's axis.
When these ancient scientists were born.Ptolemy: His Almagest set out an Earth-centred model of the heavens that astronomers trusted for about 1,400 years.
When these ancient scientists were born.Hypatia: This Alexandrian mathematician and philosopher taught a wide circle of students before a mob killed her in 415.
When these ancient scientists were born.Aryabhata: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him; he also suggested that the Earth rotates.
When these ancient scientists were born.Brahmagupta: His 628 treatise gave the first known rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers.
When these ancient scientists were born.Fibonacci: He brought Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe in 1202, and the sequence named for him came from a rabbit-breeding puzzle.
When these ancient scientists were born.Roger Bacon: The English friar urged learning through experiment, and wrote about lenses and spectacles; he was nicknamed 'Doctor Mirabilis'.

Real and fictional vessels by length.X-wing fighter: Its wingspan is about 12 m, so the fighter is smaller than a bus. Rebel pilots flew these into the Death Star trench.
Real and fictional vessels by length.Columbus's Santa Maria: Columbus's flagship ran aground on Christmas Day 1492 off Hispaniola. Its timbers were used to build a fort, La Navidad.
Real and fictional vessels by length.Millennium Falcon: Han Solo claimed it made the Kessel Run in less than twelve parsecs, though a parsec measures distance, not time. The ship's shape was inspired by a hamburger.
Real and fictional vessels by length.Noah's Ark: The Bible describes it as 300 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high. A cubit was roughly a forearm's length, about 45 cm.
Real and fictional vessels by length.The Titanic: It sank in 1912 on its maiden voyage after hitting an iceberg. At 269 m, it was the largest moving object built by humans at that time.
Real and fictional vessels by length.USS Enterprise (Star Trek TOS): Designed by Matt Jefferies, the ship from the 1960s series has a saucer and two nacelles. Its 1701 registry number was chosen to look right on screen.
Real and fictional vessels by length.Nimitz-class aircraft carrier: These nuclear-powered carriers carry around 60 aircraft and a crew of over 5,000. They can run for decades before refuelling.
Real and fictional vessels by length.Symphony of the Seas: Royal Caribbean's giant cruise ship carries over 6,000 passengers. It has a park, a zip line and a robot bartender on board.
Real and fictional vessels by length.Imperial Star Destroyer: The wedge-shaped warship appears in the opening shot of A New Hope, overwhelming the rebel ship above it. It has become a cinematic image of power.
Real and fictional vessels by length.The Death Star (first): This moon-sized station could destroy planets with its superlaser. Its trench design was famously a fatal weakness.

Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Sleeping: Your brain keeps burning roughly a fifth of your body's energy even while you sleep, so the body is never truly idle.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Watching TV: Barely above sleeping, which is why a TV marathon does little for energy balance, whatever the snacks.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Strolling slowly: The '10,000 steps' idea began with a 1960s Japanese pedometer called Manpo-kei, literally the '10,000 steps meter'.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Brisk walking: A brisk pace works up a light sweat while staying gentle on the joints, which is why it's the classic everyday workout.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Shoveling snow: It is vigorous enough to strain a sedentary person's heart, and doctors regularly warn about snow-shoveling heart attacks.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Singles tennis: Doubles burns noticeably less than singles, because partners share the court and run far shorter distances.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Jogging (10 km/h): Bill Bowerman, who later co-founded Nike, helped popularize the word 'jogging' with his 1966 book on the subject.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Fast jump rope: Boxers rely on it for conditioning, because it builds stamina and footwork, and a few minutes leaves most people breathless.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Running (16 km/h): This is roughly a six-minute-mile pace, which is hard for most recreational runners to sustain.
Calories burned per hour (70 kg person).Running (22 km/h): Elite marathoners hold about 20 to 21 km/h for the full 42 km, so this pace would be a sprint for most people.

River and lake animals by weight.Dragonfly: Dragonflies spend most of their lives as underwater nymphs, sometimes for years, before emerging to fly for just weeks. They catch prey mid-air with great accuracy.
River and lake animals by weight.Kingfisher: It plunges into water to spear small fish. Its streamlined beak shape inspired the design of Japan's Shinkansen bullet train nose.
River and lake animals by weight.Water vole: The real animal behind Ratty in The Wind in the Willows, it has declined sharply in Britain, largely because of introduced American mink.
River and lake animals by weight.Platypus: This egg-laying mammal has a bill packed with electrical sensors to find prey, and males have venomous spurs on their hind legs.
River and lake animals by weight.Atlantic salmon: Salmon return to the river where they hatched, guided by smell, to spawn. They can leap waterfalls on the way upstream.
River and lake animals by weight.Otter: Otters have the densest fur of any animal, with up to a million hairs per square inch of skin, and this keeps them warm in cold water.
River and lake animals by weight.Beaver: Beavers build dams that create ponds, changing whole landscapes. Their front teeth keep growing and are coated with iron, which is why they look orange.
River and lake animals by weight.Capybara: The world's biggest rodent is a calm, social animal that other species often sit on. It can hold its breath for several minutes underwater.
River and lake animals by weight.Manatee: Nicknamed sea cows, these gentle grazers can eat a tenth of their body weight daily. Some live in freshwater rivers and are thought to have inspired mermaid legends.
River and lake animals by weight.Hippopotamus: Hippos secrete a reddish oily fluid that works as a sunscreen. They are very dangerous and kill more people in Africa each year than lions do.

Making butter, step by step.Milk the cow: A cow can give about 25 litres of milk a day. Fresh milk is mostly water, with only about four per cent fat, which is what butter is made of.
Making butter, step by step.Let the cream rise: Fat globules are lighter than water, so they float to the top of standing milk. Today a machine called a separator does it far faster.
Making butter, step by step.Skim off the cream: The thick layer on top is skimmed away with a ladle. Cream usually holds about a third fat, and the milk left behind is skimmed milk.
Making butter, step by step.Chill the cream: Many butter makers cool the cream and let it ripen. Cultured butter, made from soured cream, has a tangier flavour popular in Europe.
Making butter, step by step.Churn it hard: Churning or whipping smashes the fat globules so that their membranes break. They stick together as the cream thickens and turns lumpy.
Making butter, step by step.Butter clumps form: The cream first whips, then suddenly separates into yellow grains of butter and thin liquid. A few more turns and the grains gather into lumps.
Making butter, step by step.Pour off the buttermilk: The thin liquid left behind is traditional buttermilk. Today's cultured buttermilk in shops is usually made differently, with bacteria added to milk.
Making butter, step by step.Rinse in cold water: Washing removes leftover buttermilk, which would turn the butter sour. Cold water also firms up the butter.
Making butter, step by step.Work in some salt: Salt adds flavour and acts as a preservative, which mattered a lot before fridges. Unsalted butter is favoured for baking so the cook controls the saltiness.
Making butter, step by step.Pat into a block: Butter is shaped by hand or with wooden paddles. Traditional dairies pressed it into moulds, often stamped with a farm's pattern.

Disney's Frozen, in story order.Elsa's magic hurts young Anna: Frozen (2013) is loosely based on Hans Christian Andersen's 1844 fairy tale The Snow Queen.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Elsa's coronation: Arendelle's look was inspired by Norway, with its fjords, wooden stave churches and Bergen's colourful waterfront.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Anna gets engaged to Hans: Hans is a prince of the Southern Isles, and his quick engagement to Anna plays on the fairy-tale love-at-first-sight trope.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Elsa flees, Arendelle freezes: Real snowflakes have six-fold symmetry because of the way water molecules arrange themselves, which Elsa's ice palace echoes.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.\"Let It Go\": Let It Go won the Oscar for Best Original Song; Idina Menzel sang it and Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez wrote it.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Anna teams up with Kristoff: Kristoff's job as an ice harvester is a real 19th-century trade where blocks were cut from frozen lakes and sold.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.They meet Olaf: Olaf is voiced by Josh Gad, and his song In Summer was a comic highlight.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Elsa strikes Anna's heart: Trolls appear in Norse and Scandinavian folklore, living in mountains and under bridges, as Grand Pabbie does.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Hans shows his true colors: Hans's betrayal was a rare Disney twist, because the film had hidden him as a charming romantic lead.
Disney's Frozen, in story order.Anna's sacrifice thaws all: Frozen became the highest-grossing animated film of its time, earning well over a billion dollars.

Famous Indians, by birth year.Rabindranath Tagore: He became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Swami Vivekananda: His 1893 speech opening with 'Sisters and brothers of America' at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago made him famous.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Mahatma Gandhi: His 1930 Salt March of about 240 miles protested a British salt tax and became a landmark of nonviolent resistance.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Srinivasa Ramanujan: A self-taught mathematician from Madras, he sent theorems to Cambridge's G. H. Hardy and was elected to the Royal Society.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Jawaharlal Nehru: India's first prime minister held the post from independence until his death, and his birthday is celebrated as Children's Day.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Satyajit Ray: The Bengali filmmaker behind the Apu Trilogy received an honorary Oscar and was also a writer, illustrator and composer.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Lata Mangeshkar: Called the 'Nightingale of India', she recorded songs in many languages and is said to have sung for thousands of films.
Famous Indians, by birth year.A. P. J. Abdul Kalam: A rocket scientist known as the 'Missile Man', he later served as India's president and was much loved as the 'People's President'.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Sachin Tendulkar: He scored 100 international centuries, a record, and debuted for India as a teenager, playing cricket at the top level for 24 years.
Famous Indians, by birth year.Virat Kohli: Captain of India's cricket team who led the under-19 side to a World Cup win, he is known for chasing down huge scores.
